result:
There is a strange freedom in being told "write about whatever you want."

Most of the time, writing has a purpose. An email has to convey information. A story has to have a plot. An argument has to convince. But when someone just opens a door and says "go," you stand there for a second, blinking in the sunlight, unsure which way to run first.

So let's run in a few directions at once.

I want to start with an idea that has been quietly haunting me: that human beings are not really living *in* the world, but that the world is living *in* us.

Think about it. Your entire experience of reality - every tree you've ever seen, every song you've ever loved, every person you've ever missed - has happened inside the private theater of your consciousness. You've never actually touched the outside world directly. You've only ever touched the *model* of it your brain builds for you, second by second, using scraps of light, vibration, pressure, and chemistry.

It sounds isolating at first, like we're all locked alone in our heads. But I think it's the opposite. Because if the universe only becomes real *as experience*, then you are not a small thing inside a big universe. You are one of the places where the big universe wakes up and looks around.

Every person is a different vantage point the cosmos has grown for itself. Your eyes are literally the universe observing itself - made from the same carbon forged in dying stars, using light that traveled eight minutes from the sun, processed by a brain that runs on electricity. When you look at the ocean and feel moved, that's not you looking at nature. That's nature looking at nature and feeling moved.

And maybe that's why connection with other people feels so important, so sacred. We're all separate theaters showing separate movies, and sometimes, for a moment, the doors open and we can glimpse each other's screen. When someone truly listens to you, or when you laugh until your stomach hurts with a friend, or when you fall in love, it feels profound because it *is* profound: two isolated universes have found a way to overlap.

Speaking of overlapping, I have a theory that time doesn't actually pass the way we think it does.

We imagine time like a river, carrying us forward. The past is behind us, the future is ahead, and the present is a little boat we're all sitting in. But what if that's backwards?

What if time is still, and it's *we* who are moving? Or more accurately, what if time is the way we experience change, not a thing that exists on its own?

Consider memory. The past doesn't exist anywhere except as traces in the present - as photographs, as neural pathways, as stories we tell. The future doesn't exist anywhere except as prediction in the present - as plans, as worries, as hopes. The only thing you have ever directly lived is *now*, this thin, razor's edge of a moment. And yet, that "now" is all you need, because it's incredibly deep.

Inside a single second, you can remember your childhood dog, feel anxious about tomorrow's meeting, taste the coffee on your tongue, and hear the traffic outside. The present isn't a point. It's a field. It contains echoes of what was and seeds of what will be.

I love that about being human. We are time-travelers by default. We live with one foot in memory and one foot in imagination, while our bodies stay faithfully in the present. No wonder we feel stretched sometimes.

If we are these time-traveling universes, then what do we do with our brief turn on stage? That's the question we all circle, whether we say it out loud or not.

For a long time, I thought the answer had to be something big. Leave a legacy. Build something that lasts. Become known. Change the world. And there's nothing wrong with ambition - the desire to make a mark is deeply human, it's part of our wanting to matter, to not be forgotten.

But the older I get, or the more I observe people who genuinely seem at peace, the more I think we've misunderstood what "big" means.

A big life is not necessarily a famous life. A big life can be a deep one.

You can change the world by raising a child with kindness so that they go on to be kind to a thousand others. You can change the world by being the friend who texts back, the neighbor who shovels the extra driveway, the stranger who actually makes eye contact and smiles in the grocery store line. You can change the world by paying attention.

Attention is the real currency. Where you put your attention, your life grows.

If you pay attention to resentments, they grow. If you pay attention to beauty - really stop and look at the way light falls through leaves, or listen to the way someone's voice softens when they talk about what they love - then beauty grows. Not just around you, but *in* you.

We talk a lot about finding meaning, as if it's buried like treasure. But maybe meaning isn't found. Maybe it's *made*, moment by moment, by what we choose to notice and nurture.

Here's something small and practical that contains all of this philosophy: learn to make something with your hands.

Cook a meal from scratch. Plant herbs on your windowsill and keep them alive. Knit a scarf, even a lopsided one. Fix a wobbly chair. Write a letter by hand. We spend so much of our lives in the abstract - in emails and feeds and notifications, pushing symbols around on glass screens. It starves a part of us that needs to see direct cause and effect, to touch something real and say, "I did that. I helped that exist."

My favorite kind of people are what I call "quiet enthusiasts." They're not trying to impress you. They're just lit up from within by something they love. The person at the party who can talk for twenty minutes about sourdough starter or vintage telescopes or why this particular trail is the best in autumn. Their eyes get bright. They use their hands when they talk. They have given themselves permission to care, unironically, about something. It's infectious. It's a reminder that joy is not a luxury; it's a practice.

And that might be the most rebellious thing you can do in a world that wants you anxious and numb and always shopping: genuinely enjoy your life.

Not in an Instagram-perfect, everything-is-amazing way. But in a real way. Let the morning coffee count. Let the sunset count. Let the conversation with your sister count. Let your own weird sense of humor count.

Because the truth is, you don't have to be extraordinary to have an extraordinary experience of being alive. You just have to be *present* for it.

We get this one life. Not a rehearsal, not a draft you'll edit later. This is it. The messy first try. The body you have, the family you have, the history you have. And for all its flaws and heartbreaks, it's also miraculous. You are a temporary arrangement of stardust that learned to read and laugh and wonder if there's more.

There is more, but not somewhere else. It's here. Folded into the ordinary.

So if you have been waiting for permission to write that poem, to take that walk, to forgive that person, to start that project, to say "I love you" first - consider this your permission slip.

Write freely. Live freely. Pay attention to what is good and real and try to make a little more of it before you go.

The door was opened for us. Let's not just stand there blinking.

Let's run.
